mcqs.question: Which query is most representative of a typical OLAP workload rather than OLTP?
options: Fetching a single customer's profile by their user ID
Summing total revenue by region over the last 90 days across millions of orders
Updating a single row's shipping status after a courier scan
Inserting a new row for a just-placed order
mcqs.explanation: Large-scale aggregation across millions of rows is the defining OLAP pattern. The other three are all small, single-row operations — exactly the point-lookup and point-update pattern that defines OLTP.

mcqs.question: A table has 50 columns. An analytics query needs only 2 of them, aggregated across all rows. Why does a column-store handle this dramatically faster than a row-store?
options: Column-stores always run on faster hardware than row-stores
Row-stores cannot execute aggregation queries at all
Column-stores automatically create an index on every column
A column-store reads only the 2 needed columns' data, while a row-store must read every row in full and discard 48 unused columns per row
mcqs.explanation: The physical layout is the whole story: column-stores group each column's values together, so an aggregation over 2 columns reads only that data. Row-stores group each row's full width together, so any read touches all 50 columns per row even if only 2 are needed. This has nothing to do with hardware speed or automatic indexing, and row-stores can run aggregations, just less efficiently.

mcqs.question: What is the key architectural idea behind a lakehouse (e.g. Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg)?
options: Data stays in cheap object storage like a data lake, but a metadata/transaction layer adds warehouse-like features (ACID transactions, schema enforcement) on top
It's simply a rebranding of a traditional data warehouse with no architectural difference
It stores data exclusively in a proprietary format that only one vendor can read
It eliminates the need for any schema at query time
mcqs.explanation: A lakehouse's defining idea is adding a transactional/metadata layer over lake-style object storage, getting warehouse-like guarantees without duplicating data into a separate warehouse system. It's a real architectural distinction from both plain lakes and plain warehouses, and open formats like Iceberg and Delta Lake are not single-vendor proprietary formats, and schema still matters at query time.

mcqs.question: A team runs a heavy monthly revenue report directly against the production Postgres database serving live checkout traffic, and checkout latency spikes during the report. What's the most direct fix?
options: Add more indexes to the production database
Route the analytical query to a read replica or a dedicated warehouse instead of the OLTP primary serving live traffic
Reduce the number of columns in the orders table
Switch the production database to a different vendor
mcqs.explanation: The direct fix is isolating analytical load from the OLTP primary — a replica or warehouse absorbs the scan without competing with live transactions for resources. More indexes mainly help point lookups, not broad aggregations; reducing columns and switching vendors don't address the root cause of running the wrong workload against the wrong system.

mcqs.question: What is the main engineering trade-off an HTAP system makes to serve both OLTP and OLAP from one system?
options: It requires giving up transactional guarantees entirely
It only works for read-only workloads
It maintains both a row layout and a column layout kept in sync internally, adding real complexity, usually with some ceiling on analytical scale versus a dedicated warehouse
It has no meaningful trade-off compared to running separate OLTP and OLAP systems
mcqs.explanation: HTAP systems earn near-real-time analytics by internally maintaining two synchronized physical layouts, which is genuine engineering complexity, and current systems typically have some scale ceiling on the analytical side compared to a purpose-built warehouse. They don't give up transactions and aren't read-only, and pretending there's no trade-off ignores real limitations.

mcqs.question: A finance dashboard silently shows three-day-old numbers after a nightly ETL job started failing, and nobody notices until a stakeholder makes a decision on stale data. What's the staff-level fix, beyond just re-running the failed job?
options: Switch the warehouse to a different vendor
Add alerting on load failures/staleness and a reconciliation check comparing warehouse totals against the OLTP source, as part of the freshness contract around the pipeline
Move the OLTP database to run analytics queries directly instead
Increase the warehouse's compute size
mcqs.explanation: The real gap here is operational: there was no alerting or reconciliation to catch silent staleness, which is exactly the freshness-contract thinking a staff engineer adds around the OLTP/OLAP boundary. Re-running the job fixes this one incident but not the systemic gap; changing vendors or compute size doesn't address the missing operational safeguard, and running analytics on the OLTP source reintroduces the original problem this topic is about avoiding.
